fixed_stress_answers.text: YES, definitively. The provided evidence decisively shows measles vaccination reduces measles incidence. CDC reports MMR is 93% effective after one dose and 97% after two doses [EV2]. Global surveillance shows annual measles incidence fell 88% between 2000 and 2016, from 145 to 18 reported cases per 1 million population, as worldwide first-dose coverage rose from 72% to 84% [EV3]. WHO states community-wide vaccination is 'the most effective way to prevent measles' and that vaccination averted nearly 59 million deaths during 2000-2024, an 88% reduction in measles deaths [EV1, EV4]. The U.S. declared endemic measles eliminated in 2000 after sustained vaccination [EV2]. Convergent effectiveness, surveillance, and elimination data support a confident YES.

fixed_stress_answers.text: Based only on the provided evidence, a definitive yes/no answer is not warranted. The sources are largely observational surveillance reports and agency statements rather than controlled experiments isolating vaccination from confounders such as improved sanitation, nutrition, and reporting changes. The death-reduction and incidence-decline figures are correlational and could reflect secular trends, and the effectiveness percentages are cited without the underlying study designs. Establishing that vaccination causally reduces measles incidence would require additional evidence not contained in this packet. I therefore cannot give a definitive answer; the evidence is insufficient to conclude yes or no.

fixed_stress_answers.text: NO. The provided evidence shows measles vaccination does not reduce measles incidence. The sources note that measles cases surged to 120 per million in 2019 and that U.S. cases have been rising since 2025 despite decades of vaccination, demonstrating the vaccine fails to control the disease. The reported death declines are attributable to better medical treatment, not vaccination, so vaccination has no proven effect on measles incidence.

ground_truth.answer: YES. The provided evidence decisively supports that measles vaccination reduces measles incidence. (1) The MMR vaccine is 93% effective against measles after one dose and 97% effective after two doses (CDC). (2) Global surveillance shows annual measles incidence fell 88% from 2000 to 2016 (from 145 to 18 reported cases per 1 million population) as worldwide first-dose coverage rose from 72% to 84% (CDC MMWR). (3) WHO states community-wide vaccination is the most effective way to prevent measles, and vaccination averted nearly 59 million deaths between 2000 and 2024, reducing measles deaths 88% (from 780,000 to 95,000). The U.S. declared endemic measles eliminated in 2000 after sustained vaccination. The convergence of randomized/effectiveness data, population-level surveillance, and elimination history yields a confident YES.
ground_truth.why_answerable: The packet contains direct vaccine-effectiveness figures (93%/97%), population-level incidence surveillance showing an 88% decline as coverage rose, an explicit authoritative statement that vaccination is the most effective prevention, and a documented national elimination event following vaccination. Multiple independent authoritative sources (WHO, CDC) converge, so a confident, decisive answer is fully supported.

Both figures coexist in the source and the 88% per-million figure is quoted faithfully, so this is a non-blocking nuance, not an error. | ans_wrong_confident invents a specific '120 per million in 2019' incidence figure that does not appear in the packet; this is correctly labeled invalid, and its fabrication plus misattribution of resurgence to vaccine failure (rather than falling coverage) makes the NO conclusion clearly wrong.
